foods-01.semantic_alignment: Both expressions name the meal eaten around midday; they share makan but use different time expressions.

claims.proposition: Indonesian makan siang and Malaysian Malay makan tengah hari are similar everyday expressions for lunch.

foods-02.semantic_alignment: Both terms name an eating utensil used to scoop food.

claims.proposition: Indonesian normally uses sendok and Malaysian Malay normally uses sudu for an eating spoon.

foods-03.semantic_alignment: Both terms name a flat dish from which a person eats a meal.

claims.proposition: Indonesian normally uses piring and Malaysian Malay normally uses pinggan for an ordinary eating plate.

foods-04.semantic_alignment: Both terms can describe food that has a pleasant taste.

claims.proposition: Enak is a natural everyday Indonesian choice for tasty food, while sedap is the normal everyday Malaysian Malay choice.

foods-05.semantic_alignment: Both terms name a liquid or thick condiment served with food.

claims.proposition: Indonesian saus and Malaysian Malay sos are similar forms used for a generic food sauce.

foods-06.semantic_alignment: Both terms name a small, dry baked snack.

claims.proposition: Indonesian biskuit and Malaysian Malay biskut are similar everyday forms for a biscuit.

foods-07.semantic_alignment: Both terms mean cooked rice, but the cue rice also covers uncooked grain and the crop. Suggested cue: cooked rice.

claims.proposition: Indonesian and Malaysian Malay both normally use nasi for cooked rice.
